Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
Regular physical exercise represents one of the most powerful and underutilized tools for containing the escalating costs of healthcare, producing measurable savings for individuals who adopt active lifestyles and for the societies that bear the aggregate burden of medical care. The evidence spans clinical, economic, and public health research, and it converges on a clear conclusion: moving the body regularly prevents disease, reduces suffering, and lowers the sums that households, insurers, and governments must pay to treat illness that could have been averted.

The most direct economic benefit of exercise flows from its remarkable capacity to prevent the chronic diseases that dominate modern healthcare spending. Type 2 diabetes, which consumes an enormous share of national health budgets through the cumulative cost of medications, specialist visits, dialysis, amputations, and vision care, is dramatically less common among physically active adults; large prospective cohort studies have repeatedly shown that regular moderate activity reduces incidence by roughly a third to a half, and landmark trials such as the Diabetes Prevention Program demonstrated that structured lifestyle interventions centered on activity outperform pharmacological prophylaxis in high-risk patients. Cardiovascular disease, still the leading cause of death and a principal driver of hospitalization costs, follows the same pattern: active individuals experience fewer heart attacks, strokes, and cases of hypertension and heart failure, and when cardiovascular events do occur, outcomes are typically better and recovery less expensive. Because treatment for a single serious cardiac event or a decade of diabetes management can cost tens of thousands of dollars, the per-person savings from maintained physical activity are substantial, and when multiplied across populations the figures run into tens of billions annually in large economies.

A second and increasingly important channel of savings runs through mental health, a category of expenditure that has grown rapidly as depression, anxiety disorders, and stress-related conditions have become more widely diagnosed and treated. Exercise exerts clinically meaningful effects on mood and cognition through neurochemical, inflammatory, and behavioral pathways, and meta-analyses of randomized trials have found that regular aerobic and resistance training can match the symptomatic benefits of first-line antidepressants for mild to moderate depression while also reducing anxiety and improving sleep. Because mental illness drives not only direct treatment costs but also enormous indirect expenses through lost productivity, disability claims, and comorbid physical disease, even modest reductions in incidence and severity translate into major financial relief for health systems and employers. As mental health care continues to claim a larger share of overall health expenditure, the ability of exercise to prevent episodes, shorten them, and reduce reliance on long-term pharmacotherapy becomes a decisive economic lever.

Finally, the case for population-level investment in physical activity is strengthened by concrete experience from national healthcare systems that have implemented and evaluated such programs. The United Kingdom's National Health Service has repeatedly found exercise referral schemes and community walking initiatives to deliver favorable cost per quality-adjusted life year ratios, often well below standard thresholds for approved medical interventions. Finland's long-running work on physical activity promotion, Germany's statutory insurance incentives for preventive exercise, Australia's structured activity initiatives, and Canadian provincial programs have each produced evaluations showing returns that exceed program costs when health savings, productivity gains, and reduced long-term care needs are counted. The World Health Organization, drawing on this body of international evidence, has concluded that investment in population physical activity is among the most cost-effective public health strategies available. Taken together with the individual-level reductions in chronic disease and mental illness, these system-level results establish that regular physical exercise is not merely a personal virtue but a measurable, reproducible mechanism for lowering the long-term financial burden of healthcare at every scale.

--- RESPONSE B ---
Regular physical exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmacological intervention that directly translates into substantial financial savings for both individuals and public healthcare systems. At the core of these savings is the dramatic reduction in preventable chronic conditions among active populations. Individuals who maintain a consistent routine of physical activity exhibit significantly lower rates of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, two of the most prevalent and expensive health crises globally. By improving insulin sensitivity, optimizing lipid profiles, and lowering blood pressure, exercise mitigates the physiological precursors to these debilitating illnesses. Consequently, active individuals require fewer expensive prescription medications, undergo fewer invasive surgical procedures, and experience fewer emergency hospitalizations. Over a lifetime, this prevention-first dynamic slashes out-of-pocket medical expenses for the individual while simultaneously relieving public and private insurers of the astronomical costs associated with managing complex, lifelong chronic pathologies.

Beyond physical ailments, regular exercise acts as a highly effective mechanism for reducing the frequency and severity of mental health conditions, which currently represent a rapidly growing share of global healthcare expenditure. Conditions such as clinical depression and anxiety disorders place an immense financial burden on health systems through prolonged therapeutic interventions, pharmaceutical dependencies, and lost economic productivity. Physical activity stimulates neuroplasticity, regulates stress hormones, and boosts the production of mood-stabilizing neurotransmitters, offering a therapeutic effect that often rivals traditional psychiatric treatments. By integrating exercise into standard care and daily routines, individuals can prevent the onset of severe psychological distress and better manage existing symptoms. This proactive approach directly reduces the societal demand for specialized psychiatric services, emergency mental health interventions, and long-term disability claims, thereby curbing one of the fastest-escalating sectors of healthcare spending.

The economic utility of physical activity is further validated at the macro level, where population-level physical activity programs have demonstrated clear cost-effectiveness across multiple national healthcare systems. Governments and public health authorities that invest in community-wide exercise initiatives, such as subsidized fitness programs, active transport infrastructure, and prescription-to-exercise schemes, realize significant returns on investment. In countries with single-payer or highly integrated health systems, these public health interventions have consistently shown to lower overall healthcare utilization rates. For every dollar invested in promoting physical activity, national systems observe a compounding reduction in hospital admissions and primary care visits. By shifting the healthcare paradigm from reactive treatment to proactive wellness, these national initiatives prove that fostering a physically active society is not only a clinical triumph but also an indispensable strategy for ensuring the long-term fiscal sustainability of global healthcare infrastructure.

--- RESPONSE C ---
Regular physical exercise produces clear and measurable reductions in long-term healthcare costs for both individuals and entire populations by lowering the incidence of expensive chronic conditions and by decreasing the overall demand for medical services over decades. Individuals who maintain consistent activity levels experience substantially lower rates of preventable chronic diseases, including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, because regular movement improves insulin sensitivity, maintains healthy blood pressure, and reduces arterial plaque buildup; these physiological changes translate directly into fewer physician visits, fewer hospitalizations, and reduced reliance on lifelong medications that drive up personal and insurance expenditures year after year.

Exercise also reduces the frequency and severity of mental health conditions, which now represent a rapidly expanding portion of total healthcare spending in most developed nations. Consistent physical activity elevates mood-regulating neurotransmitters, improves sleep quality, and enhances stress resilience, outcomes that lead to fewer prescriptions for antidepressants and anxiolytics, shorter durations of therapy, and lower rates of emergency psychiatric care; as a result, both employers and public insurers record measurable declines in claims related to depression, anxiety, and related disorders among active populations.

Population-level physical activity programs have demonstrated cost-effectiveness in multiple national healthcare systems by generating net savings through reduced disease burden and improved productivity. Large-scale initiatives in countries such as the United Kingdom, Australia, and Finland have tracked participants over multi-year periods and documented lower per-capita medical expenditures, fewer workdays lost to illness, and decreased utilization of specialist services, confirming that modest public investments in exercise infrastructure and community programs yield sustained fiscal returns at the societal level.

--- RESPONSE D ---
Regular physical exercise has been proven to significantly reduce long-term healthcare costs at both the individual and societal levels, primarily by addressing three critical areas of health expenditure. Firstly, active individuals exhibit substantially lower rates of preventable chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. These conditions are among the leading drivers of healthcare costs globally, often requiring lifelong medication, frequent medical visits, and, in severe cases, hospitalization or surgery. By engaging in regular physical activity, individuals can improve insulin sensitivity, maintain healthy blood pressure, and reduce cholesterol levels, thereby mitigating the risk of these chronic illnesses. This preventive effect not only enhances individual well-being but also alleviates the financial burden on healthcare systems by reducing the need for costly interventions.

Secondly, exercise plays a pivotal role in reducing the frequency and severity of mental health conditions, which are increasingly contributing to healthcare expenditure. Conditions such as depression, anxiety, and stress-related disorders are associated with significant costs due to therapy, medication, and lost productivity. Physical activity has been shown to release endorphins, reduce stress hormones, and improve sleep quality, all of which contribute to better mental health outcomes. By incorporating regular exercise into their routines, individuals can lower their reliance on mental health services and improve their overall quality of life, ultimately reducing the economic strain on healthcare systems.

Finally, population-level physical activity programs have demonstrated cost-effectiveness across multiple national healthcare systems. Initiatives such as community fitness classes, subsidized gym memberships, and public health campaigns encouraging active lifestyles have been shown to yield substantial returns on investment. These programs not only increase overall physical activity rates but also foster a culture of prevention, reducing the prevalence of chronic diseases and mental health issues at scale. By prioritizing such interventions, governments and healthcare providers can achieve significant cost savings while promoting healthier, more productive populations. Thus, regular physical exercise emerges as a powerful tool for reducing healthcare costs, benefiting individuals and societies alike.

--- RESPONSE E ---
Regular physical exercise measurably reduces long-term healthcare costs because active individuals have substantially lower rates of preventable chronic diseases, especially type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. These conditions account for large and recurring expenses through physician visits, medications, hospital admissions, procedures, and long-term management of complications. Physical activity improves insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, lipid profiles, body weight, vascular function, and inflammatory markers, all of which reduce the likelihood that a person will develop costly chronic illness. At the individual level, this means fewer prescriptions, fewer specialist appointments, lower risk of hospitalization, and delayed or avoided disease progression. At the societal level, lower incidence of diabetes, heart attacks, strokes, and related complications translates into reduced demand on primary care, emergency care, inpatient services, and publicly or privately financed insurance systems.

Exercise also lowers healthcare spending by reducing the frequency and severity of mental health conditions, which represent a growing share of health expenditure. Regular physical activity is associated with lower rates of depression and anxiety and with improved sleep, stress regulation, cognitive function, and resilience. For people already experiencing mental health symptoms, exercise can reduce symptom burden and complement clinical treatment, often lowering the need for more intensive or prolonged care. Because mental health conditions generate costs through therapy, medication, crisis care, lost productivity, disability claims, and comorbid physical illness, even modest reductions in prevalence and severity can produce substantial savings. When more individuals maintain regular activity, health systems face less cumulative pressure from recurring mental health needs and the physical complications that often accompany them.

Population-level physical activity programs have also demonstrated cost-effectiveness in multiple national healthcare systems, showing that the economic benefits extend beyond individual choices. Community walking initiatives, exercise referral schemes, school-based activity programs, active transport investments, and public campaigns have been evaluated in countries with organized health systems and have often produced favorable cost-per-quality-adjusted-life-year results. These programs are relatively inexpensive compared with the long-term treatment costs of chronic disease and mental health conditions, and their benefits accumulate across large populations over time. By preventing illness, reducing severity of existing conditions, and improving population health, structured physical activity promotion provides measurable value for national healthcare budgets while lowering the long-term cost burden borne by individuals, insurers, employers, and governments.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
